Senses.Explanation: To plunge head-first into a glue pot is to turn an apparently freeing move into an entrapment of one’s own making. Chan masters use the image when a smile, question, or proposed recognition sticks the participant more firmly in the very position being tested. Chonghua Neng applies it to Kasyapa’s smile after the flower is raised. Yunwai Xingze throws it at a questioner who asks where a universal gate of liberation is released. Senses.Explanation: As a Chan record heading and event label, 示眾 means to address or instruct the assembled community. The Bamboo Chamber preface lists 上堂示眾 among Dawei's teaching compositions, showing its institutional genre use. A Nanquan case uses 示眾曰 to introduce his public challenge, while Weilin's record says that several practitioners requested 示眾 and then gives his extended instruction. The phrase can therefore designate either the event or its recorded textual unit; in both uses the defining action is public instruction.

Senses.Explanation: This is a fixed Chan epithet for Bodhidharma, not a productive description of any elderly foreigner. Its literally missing teeth become part of a compact, often mocking name for the lineage's western founder. Wuzhun Shifan attaches the epithet to nine years facing a wall at Shaolin. Huanxi Weiyi asks what use the tooth-gapped old foreigner has for a single direct transmission and follows with a pun about knocking out the front teeth. These local predicates identify both the person and the tooth image without requiring an outside biography. Shaweng Huihai calls the figure a traveler who came ten thousand miles from the west and then divided skin and marrow among descendants. Xuefeng Kong's verse places the same epithet amid transmission language and later names Bodhidharma nearby. Across these independent uses, the phrase remains Bodhidharma's epithet even when a master disputes or mocks what is attributed to him.
